Pericardial effusion is the accumulation of excess fluid within the pericardial space.
Cardiac tamponade is a life-threatening condition where a significant pericardial effusion causes compression of the heart, impairing its ability to fill and pump blood effectively.
Examination: goitre or neck nodes, hair and nail changes, carpal tunnel signs (Tinel, Phalen), pericardial effusion, ascites, ankle oedema, mental state and the ankle reflex relaxation time.

qs.q: Which clinical sign is characteristic of cardiac tamponade resulting from pericardial effusion?
o: Pulsus paradoxus with a drop during breath
Bounding peripheral pulses with wide pressure
Hypertension with hyperdynamic impulse
Collapsing pulse and early diastolic murmur
qs.e: Cardiac tamponade impairs ventricular filling, classically presenting with distended jugular veins, decreased heart sounds, and a pulsus paradoxus defined as a >10 mmHg drop in systolic blood pressure during inspiration. Bounding pulses are typical of aortic runoff lesions rather than tamponade.

qs.q: An 8-year-old child presents with distant heart sounds, jugular venous distension, and hypotension following a viral illness. Which chest radiographic finding is classically seen with a large pericardial effusion?
o: Water-bottle cardiac silhouette
Prominent double atrial contour
Enlarged boot-shaped heart
Notching of the posterior ribs
qs.e: A large accumulation of fluid in the pericardial space typically enlarges the cardiac silhouette into a characteristic water-bottle shape. A boot-shaped heart is classically associated with right ventricular hypertrophy in tetralogy of Fallot.

qs.q: A 45-year-old man is monitored following cardiac surgery. How does the rate of fluid accumulation typically affect the clinical manifestation of pericardial effusion?
o: Fluid accumulation rate has no bearing on ventricular filling
Rapid accumulation requires over a liter before pressure changes
Rapid accumulation of small volumes can severely impede output
Slow accumulation prevents any fluid from entering the space
qs.e: The amount of fluid required to impair filling depends on the rate of accumulation and compliance; rapid accumulation of as little as 150 ml can severely impede cardiac output, whereas 1000 ml over a long period may have no immediate clinical effect. The other options contradict known physiological principles of pericardial compliance.

qs.q: When is a subxiphoid thoracotomy indicated in the management of pericardial effusions or tamponade?
o: When the patient refuses local anesthesia during echocardiography
As the initial routine first-line approach for every simple serous effusion
To treat underlying essential hypertension prior to fluid aspiration
In the setting of recurrent tamponade and to remove loculated effusions
qs.e: Subxiphoid thoracotomy is performed to surgically drain fluid in recurrent tamponade, remove loculated effusions, and obtain tissue for diagnosis. It is not the standard first-line approach for simple effusions.

qs.q: A 31-year-old woman has bilateral pleural and pericardial effusions. Anti-ds-DNA is 1:512. If BUN rises to 55 mg/dL, it will most likely result from which pathologic process?
o: Amyloid deposition
Anti-glomerular basement membrane antibody
Atherosclerosis
Immune complex deposition
qs.e: SLE causes renal failure through type III hypersensitivity with immune complex deposition in glomeruli. Anti-ds-DNA is highly specific for SLE and correlates with lupus nephritis activity.

ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Pericardial effusion is excess fluid in the pericardial sac that can compress the heart, impairing filling. It often follows infection, malignancy, or systemic disease and may progress to tamponade.

sections.p: A pericardial effusion is fluid that accumulates in the pericardial space. Diagnosis is confirmed by imaging—echocardiography is first line, CT or MRI if echo is inconclusive. Clinical suspicion arises when a patient has chest pain, dyspnea, or a new distant heart sound.
b: Echocardiography: detects echo-free space, diastolic collapse of right ventricle, respiratory variation in mitral/tricuspid flow

t.b: A clear echo-free space >5 mm suggests effusion; right ventricular diastolic collapse indicates tamponade.
A globular heart shape may hint at large effusion, but is non‑specific.
Low voltage (<0.5 mV) or beat‑to‑beat variation suggests significant fluid.

sections.p: Severity is staged by size and hemodynamic impact. Small effusions are asymptomatic; large effusions can cause tamponade. The classic Beck’s triad—hypotension, muffled heart sounds, jugular venous distension—signals tamponade.

In low‑resource settings, infections dominate. Tuberculosis is the leading cause, followed by HIV, malaria, and bacterial sepsis. Non‑infectious causes include malignancy, autoimmune disease, and post‑cardiac surgery.

Patients may have chest pain, dyspnea, cough, or fatigue. Classic signs include distant heart sounds, pulsus paradoxus, and jugular venous distension. In low‑resource settings, symptoms may be vague and overlap with other illnesses.
Echocardiography is the cornerstone. When unavailable, a focused cardiac exam and chest X‑ray can guide suspicion. Lab tests help identify etiology.

t.b: Shows fluid size and right ventricular collapse.
Suggests large effusion but not specific.
Leukocytosis or anemia may point to TB or malignancy.
Elevated values support infectious or autoimmune causes.

sections.p: Rapid accumulation or large volume can precipitate cardiac tamponade, leading to shock. Chronic effusions may cause constrictive physiology. Watch for arrhythmias, hypotension, and respiratory distress.

faq.a: Yes, small effusions often have no symptoms and are found incidentally.

faq.q: Is pericardiocentesis safe in low‑resource settings?
faq.a: It is safe if performed by trained staff with basic monitoring; ultrasound guidance improves accuracy.
Use clinical exam, chest X‑ray, and basic ECG; if tamponade is suspected, proceed to pericardiocentesis based on clinical judgment.
